java.questionText: What occurs if a new class PaypalPayment attempts to implement PaymentMethod without being listed in the permits clause?
options: The code fails to compile because only classes explicitly listed in the permits clause are permitted to extend/implement a sealed type.
PaypalPayment will automatically compile as a non-sealed subclass.
The JVM throws a RuntimeException at class loading time.
PaypalPayment compiles but requires reflection to instantiate.
java.explanation: Sealed classes (JEP 409 in Java 17) restrict which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement them. Subclasses must be declared in the permits clause in the same module or package and explicitly marked final, sealed, or non-sealed. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: Why is a default branch not required in this switch expression?
options: Because the compiler knows all permitted subtypes of the sealed interface Shape and verifies that every possible subtype is exhaustively covered.
Because switch expressions in Java 21 never require default branches.
Because records automatically implement a fallback default case.
Because the JVM generates a synthetic default branch at runtime.
java.explanation: With sealed classes and pattern matching for switch, the compiler checks for exhaustiveness across all permitted subtypes. If all subtypes are handled, no default branch is needed. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: How does nested record pattern matching deconstruct the Window instance?
options: It matches the Window record, recursively extracts the topLeft Point record component, binds x and y, and binds br to bottomRight in a single step.
It uses reflection to read private fields of Point.
It creates deep copies of both Point and Window objects on the heap.
It throws NullPointerException if bottomRight is null.
java.explanation: Java 21 Record Patterns (JEP 440) enable nested deconstruction patterns that test whether a target is an instance of a record and extract its component values directly into local pattern variables. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What is the execution order evaluated when evaluating a switch case with a 'when' guard?
options: The pattern type is checked first; if matched, the boolean expression in the 'when' clause is evaluated before executing the branch.
The 'when' expression is evaluated first before checking the object type.
All 'when' expressions across all cases are evaluated concurrently.
The compiler requires all 'when' guards to be pure compile-time constants.
java.explanation: Java 21 Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441) allows 'when' clauses (guarded patterns). The runtime tests the type pattern first, and only if it matches does it evaluate the conditional guard. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What adverse performance impact occurs during the blocking query inside the synchronized block?
options: The virtual thread cannot be unmounted from its underlying carrier platform thread because synchronized blocks currently pin the carrier thread.
The JVM terminates the virtual thread with an IllegalMonitorStateException.
The database driver automatically upgrades the connection to non-blocking I/O.
The carrier thread is duplicated by the OS scheduler.
java.explanation: In Java 21, when a virtual thread performs a blocking operation while holding a synchronized monitor lock or executing a JNI native frame, it is 'pinned' to its carrier thread, preventing other virtual threads from using that carrier. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: Why does switching from synchronized to ReentrantLock prevent carrier thread pinning?
options: java.util.concurrent locks are implemented in Java using AQS parking, allowing the virtual thread scheduler to unmount the virtual thread cleanly during waits.
ReentrantLock disables all OS thread synchronization.
ReentrantLock allocates carrier threads dynamically in C++.
ReentrantLock executes all I/O operations in memory without blocking.
java.explanation: ReentrantLock relies on LockSupport.park(), which integrates directly with the Virtual Thread scheduler to unmount the virtual thread and yield the carrier thread back to the ForkJoinPool. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: Why are Scoped Values superior to ThreadLocal when handling high volumes of virtual threads?
options: Scoped Values are immutable, bound to a specific execution scope, and shared by reference across subtasks without memory bloat or risk of thread-local memory leaks.
Scoped Values store data in CPU hardware registers.
ThreadLocal requires external native libraries on virtual threads.
Scoped Values permit global mutable updates from any thread.
java.explanation: ThreadLocal creates mutable copies across threads, leading to unbounded memory consumption and leak risks when inheriting across millions of virtual threads. ScopedValue is immutable and lexically bounded. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: If fetchAccount(id) fails with a RuntimeException, what does ShutdownOnFailure do with the sibling fetchOrders task?
options: It cancels the remaining unfinished subtask by interrupting its thread, ensuring no orphan threads leak or waste compute.
It allows fetchOrders to run indefinitely in the background.
It restarts fetchAccount 3 times automatically.
It forces the entire JVM to crash.
java.explanation: Structured Concurrency treats concurrent subtasks as a single unit of work. ShutdownOnFailure cancels remaining running tasks as soon as one subtask fails, preventing orphan threads. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What is the performance characteristic of the reversed() method on a SequencedCollection?
options: It returns a lightweight, reverse-ordered view of the underlying collection in O(1) time without copying elements.
It creates an entirely new deep copy of the collection taking O(N) time and memory.
It reverses the elements in-place modifying the original list.
It takes O(N log N) by sorting elements in descending order.
java.explanation: JEP 431 introduces SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap. The reversed() method provides an O(1) reverse-ordered view on top of the original collection. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: When executing this collector on a parallel stream, which characteristic flag allows multiple sub-threads to accumulate into a single shared concurrent map?
java.codeSnippet:
Collector<String, ?, Map<Integer, List<String>>> customCollector =
    Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, Collectors.toList());
options: Collector.Characteristics.CONCURRENT combined with UNORDERED.
Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH only.
Parallel streams cannot execute custom collectors.
Collector.Characteristics.SERIAL_ONLY.
java.explanation: When a Collector has CONCURRENT and UNORDERED characteristics, the parallel stream pipeline accumulates results concurrently into a single shared container without intermediate merge steps. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What transformation is applied by flatMap(Collection::stream) on the stream elements?
java.codeSnippet:
List<List<String>> nested = List.of(List.of("A", "B"), List.of("C", "D"));
List<String> result = nested.stream().flatMap(Collection::stream).toList();
options: It transforms each inner list into an individual stream of elements and flattens all resulting streams into a single unified stream.
It filters out null elements and sorts the list alphabetically.
It wraps each list into an unmodifiable collection view.
It converts the nested list into an array of strings in O(1) time.
java.explanation: flatMap maps each element to a stream of new values and then flattens all streams into a single output stream. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What capability does 'opens ... to spring.core' grant compared to 'exports'?
options: It permits deep reflective access at runtime (private fields/methods) specifically to spring.core, while keeping the package inaccessible for compile-time references.
It makes all internal classes public to every module at compile-time.
It compiles the internal package into native assembly code.
It bypasses all JVM type checks entirely.
java.explanation: In JPMS, 'exports' exposes public types at compile-time and runtime. 'opens' permits runtime deep reflection (e.g. for Spring/Hibernate dependency injection) without compile-time visibility. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: What underlying OS mechanism allows MappedByteBuffer to achieve high I/O throughput on multi-gigabyte files?
options: It maps a region of the file directly into process virtual memory, leveraging the OS page cache and demand paging without JVM heap copying.
It copies the entire file into the JVM Young Generation heap.
It disables the operating system disk cache.
It executes file reads inside CPU L1 cache.
java.explanation: FileChannel.map() uses the OS mmap() system call to map file contents directly to virtual memory addresses, allowing direct access via OS page cache with zero JVM user-space copying. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: How does Generational ZGC track references from old generation objects to young generation objects during young-only collections?
java.codeSnippet:
// -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational
// 32GB Heap with high allocation churn
options: It maintains remembered sets updated by JIT-compiled store/load barriers to identify cross-generational roots without scanning the entire old generation.
It performs a full Stop-The-World heap scan on every GC cycle.
It moves all old generation objects into off-heap memory.
It relies entirely on reference counting.
java.explanation: Generational ZGC (JEP 439 in Java 21) separates young and old generations, maintaining store barriers to record old-to-young pointers so young collections run independently with sub-millisecond pauses. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

java.questionText: In high-throughput microservice, carrier threads become starved during I/O reads. Why does this virtual thread pinning occur and how should it be refactored?
options: The virtual thread cannot unmount because it performs blocking I/O while holding a synchronized monitor lock. Refactor to ReentrantLock to allow unmounting.
The carrier thread scheduler pool size must be scaled to 50,000 threads.
Synchronized monitors cannot be used inside virtual threads and cause immediate JVM crashes.
Virtual threads cannot perform SocketChannel I/O operations without throwing IllegalStateException.
java.explanation: Under Project Loom (Java 21), a virtual thread is pinned to its carrier platform thread when executing inside a synchronized block or JNI native method. Replacing synchronized with java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock allows the Loom runtime to cleanly unmount the virtual thread upon blocking I/O.

java.questionText: When spawning 50,000 virtual threads for tenant processing, why is ScopedValue vastly superior to ThreadLocal?
options: ThreadLocal throws UnsupportedOperationException inside virtual thread runnables.
ScopedValue allocates data in CPU register L1 cache rather than JVM heap memory.
ScopedValue automatically compiles bytecode directly to C++ native instructions.
ScopedValue is immutable, shared by reference across child subtasks, and bounded to the lexical scope, preventing per-thread memory bloat and memory leaks.
java.explanation: ThreadLocal creates mutable per-thread entries in ThreadLocalMap which wastes massive heap when scaling to hundreds of thousands of virtual threads and risks leaks if remove() is omitted. ScopedValue is immutable and shared safely down the call tree.

java.questionText: If paymentClient.chargeAccount throws PaymentTimeoutException, what does StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure do to the inventory reservation subtask?
options: It rolls back the database using distributed two-phase commit.
It leaves the inventory subtask running as an orphan background thread.
It immediately calls cancel() on the scope, sending an interrupt signal to the inventory virtual thread to abort wasted execution.
It blocks indefinitely until the inventory subtask completes successfully.
java.explanation: StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure treats concurrent subtasks as a single unit of work: the first failure immediately invokes cancel() on sibling subtasks, interrupting their threads and reclaiming CPU/network resources.

java.questionText: What thread executes the `exceptionally` fallback callback when enrichMetadata throws an unchecked RuntimeException?
options: Always the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() regardless of customExecutor.
The thread that completed the upstream stage with an exception (or the submitting thread if already completed), unless exceptionallyAsync is used.
The JVM Finalizer daemon thread.
A brand new OS kernel thread spawned on demand.
java.explanation: Synchronous completion callbacks in CompletableFuture (like .exceptionally or .thenApply) execute on the thread that completes the preceding stage. To offload the fallback to a dedicated pool, Java 12 introduced .exceptionallyAsync().

java.questionText: Why does LongAdder significantly outperform AtomicLong under heavy write contention across multi-core CPUs?
options: LongAdder maintains an internal array of Cell cells hashed per-thread, reducing CAS bus-locking contention and summing only on sum() invocation.
AtomicLong synchronizes on the global class monitor lock during incrementAndGet.
LongAdder converts int primitive numbers to IEEE 754 floating points.
LongAdder uses optimistic database row locks rather than CPU instructions.
java.explanation: AtomicLong repeatedly spins CAS on a single volatile value, causing severe cache-coherence traffic across CPU cores. LongAdder stripes mutations across dynamic Cell array slots based on thread hash, eliminating contention.

java.questionText: How does Generational ZGC achieve sub-millisecond maximum pause times on large heaps up to 16TB?
java.codeSnippet:
// Options: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx7631g
// Allocation rate: 52 MB/sec
options: It uses 64-bit reference colored pointers and JIT load barriers to relocate live objects concurrently while mutator application threads are running.
It stores all heap objects in Linux shared tmpfs memory.
It disables young-to-old object promotion completely.
It performs full Stop-The-World compaction during low-traffic hours.
java.explanation: Generational ZGC embeds metadata bits (Marked0, Marked1, Remapped) directly into the 64-bit virtual memory reference pointers. When mutator threads dereference an un-relocated object, load barriers intercept it and self-heal the pointer concurrently.

java.questionText: If an allocated object is larger than 50% of the G1HeapRegionSize, where does G1GC allocate it and what is the performance impact?
java.codeSnippet:
byte[] largePayload_2490 = new byte[48 * 1024 * 1024]; // 48MB array
// G1HeapRegionSize is set to 8MB
options: The JVM rejects the allocation with BufferOverflowException.
It is compressed in JVM Metaspace until GC compaction.
It is allocated directly in a contiguous sequence of Humongous regions in the Old Generation, which can trigger premature Concurrent Mark and heap fragmentation.
It is allocated in Eden space and promoted to Survivor space during the next Young GC.
java.explanation: In G1GC, any object exceeding 50% of G1HeapRegionSize is treated as Humongous and allocated directly in Old Gen humongous regions. Frequent humongous allocations lead to rapid Old Gen filling and GC pauses. Solution: increase -XX:G1HeapRegionSize.

java.questionText: Why does continuously loading classes with new classloader instances without releasing static references trigger java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace?
options: Metaspace is stored on the OS swap partition and cannot exceed 64MB.
URLClassLoader instances are permanently pinned in CPU cache.
The Java bytecode verifier runs out of stack frames.
A classloader cannot be garbage collected if any static field or instance retains a reference to it; uncollected class metadata fills native Metaspace.
java.explanation: Classes and ClassLoader instances are strongly linked: as long as a single class, instance, or ThreadLocal reference is reachable, the entire ClassLoader and all its Metaspace metadata cannot be unloaded, exhausting MaxMetaspaceSize.

java.questionText: Why is the `volatile` keyword mandatory for thread-safe Double-Checked Locking in the Java Memory Model?
options: It stores the Resource instance in Metaspace memory.
Without volatile, synchronized blocks cannot execute concurrently.
It prevents CPU and JIT compiler instruction reordering between object memory allocation, constructor initialization, and reference assignment.
It ensures the class monitor lock is held during get() calls.
java.explanation: Object construction involves 3 steps: (1) allocate memory, (2) run constructor, (3) assign pointer. Without volatile, (3) can reorder before (2), exposing a non-null but uninitialized object to other reading threads.

java.questionText: When a bucket in ConcurrentHashMap reaches 8 colliding entries and table capacity is >= 64, what internal transformation occurs?
java.codeSnippet:
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> map_7850 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(16);
// 12 colliding keys inserted with identical hashCode()
options: The map allocates an auxiliary SkipList bucket on off-heap memory.
The map acquires a global synchronized lock across all buckets.
All entries in that bucket are discarded with ConcurrentModificationException.
The singly linked Node list is converted into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeBin) for O(log N) search complexity.
java.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap and HashMap treeify buckets when length >= TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) and capacity >= MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64). If capacity < 64, it resizes the table instead of treeifying.

java.questionText: Why can excessive DirectByteBuffer allocations trigger native OutOfMemoryError even when JVM heap space is 90% free?
java.codeSnippet:
ByteBuffer directBuf_7805 = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(38 * 1024 * 1024); // Direct off-heap buffer
// Direct buffer goes out of scope without explicit cleaning
options: The OS kills the process due to unaligned CPU SIMD registers.
Direct buffers are permanently locked by the Linux kernel.
Off-heap memory is only reclaimed when the PhantomReference Cleaner runs during GC; if heap allocation rate is low, GC is not triggered in time to free off-heap memory.
DirectByteBuffer cannot exceed the young generation Eden size.
java.explanation: DirectByteBuffer allocates native memory via malloc() and attaches a PhantomReference Cleaner. If Mutator threads allocate off-heap memory faster than Young GC triggers, native memory is exhausted before Cleaner runs. Tune with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.

spring-boot.questionText: Why is RestClient preferred over RestTemplate in Spring Boot 3.2+ for synchronous HTTP communications?
options: RestClient offers a modern, fluent API matching WebClient while working with synchronous HttpMessageConverters without requiring reactive WebFlux dependencies.
RestTemplate throws UnsupportedOperationException in Spring Boot 3.
RestClient only communicates using binary gRPC protocols.
RestClient requires an external Netty server.
spring-boot.explanation: RestClient is Spring's modern synchronous HTTP client offering a fluent builder-style API, replacing RestTemplate for new development without requiring Project Reactor. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: Why does internalSave() execute without transactional management when called from placeOrder()?
options: Direct this.internalSave() invokes the method on the target instance directly, bypassing the Spring AOP dynamic proxy interceptor chain.
@Transactional is ignored on methods named internalSave.
Spring Boot disables transactions inside Service classes by default.
The transaction is rolled back before entering the method.
spring-boot.explanation: Spring AOP advice is applied through proxy objects. Internal this.method() calls bypass the proxy wrapper. To fix: inject the proxy self-reference, use AspectJ compile-time weaving, or refactor to another bean. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: Under default Spring @Transactional configuration, why does throwing a checked exception NOT trigger a transaction rollback?
options: Spring Declarative Transactions roll back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error) by default unless rollbackFor is configured.
Checked exceptions are silently committed by database drivers.
Spring Boot transactions only roll back on OutOfMemoryError.
The database automatically catches custom checked exceptions.
spring-boot.explanation: By default, Spring transactions roll back only on unchecked exceptions. To roll back on checked exceptions, declare @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class). (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: How does @EntityGraph prevent N+1 queries when loading Department entities with lazy-loaded employees?
options: It generates a single SQL query with an INNER/LEFT JOIN to eagerly fetch the specified associated employees in a single round-trip.
It stores all Department records in Redis cache.
It disables lazy loading across all entities in the entire JVM.
It forces the database to execute background stored procedures.
spring-boot.explanation: @EntityGraph allows overriding default fetch plans on a per-query basis, instructing JPA/Hibernate to use a SQL JOIN to fetch child relationships in a single query. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: What is the core function of customJwtConverter in this Spring Security configuration?
options: It extracts customized claims (such as realm_access.roles) from the validated JWT token and maps them into GrantedAuthority objects in the SecurityContext.
It decrypts the incoming TLS TCP socket traffic.
It generates asymmetric RSA keys for every HTTP request.
It stores the user password in plaintext in session memory.
spring-boot.explanation: JwtAuthenticationConverter transforms JWT payload claims into Spring Security GrantedAuthority instances (e.g. ROLE_ADMIN), enabling method security annotations like @PreAuthorize. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: How does Micrometer Tracing maintain end-to-end trace correlation across downstream microservices?
options: By automatically injecting W3C Trace Context headers ('traceparent' and 'tracestate') into outgoing HTTP request headers via client interceptors.
By writing trace IDs to a central database on every HTTP request.
By broadcasting UDP heartbeat packets to all network switches.
By attaching trace IDs to the TCP handshake SYN packet.
spring-boot.explanation: Micrometer Tracing injects standard W3C Trace Context HTTP headers (traceparent) into downstream requests, enabling distributed tracing across microservices. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: When 6 out of 10 requests fail in the sliding window, what immediate behavior change occurs for the 11th request?
options: The circuit transitions to OPEN, immediately short-circuiting the 11th request with CallNotPermittedException without calling the downstream service.
The 11th request is queued indefinitely in memory until the service recovers.
The application server restarts the Tomcat container.
The 11th request is executed 100 times concurrently.
spring-boot.explanation: When the failure rate breaches the configured threshold, the Circuit Breaker transitions to OPEN, failing fast with CallNotPermittedException to protect downstream services. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: What is the purpose of dynamic request(n) signaling in Reactive Streams backpressure?
options: It allows the consumer to pull only the number of items it has capacity to process, preventing producer fast-push memory overflow.
It forces the publisher to run in a single thread.
It converts asynchronous streams into blocking JDBC queries.
It pauses the OS CPU clock until data arrives.
spring-boot.explanation: Backpressure in Reactive Streams (Project Reactor) allows subscribers to regulate data flow by demanding specific batch sizes via request(n), preventing buffer overflows. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

spring-boot.questionText: When processOrder is called from an external controller, why does updatePaymentStatus execute WITHOUT creating a new transaction?
options: PaymentRepository must implement AspectJ pointcuts directly.
Internal transactions are committed automatically before method entry.
Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW is deprecated in Spring Boot 3.
Spring `@Transactional` is intercepted by a dynamic proxy; internal `this` method invocations bypass the proxy interceptor.
spring-boot.explanation: Spring AOP creates a CGLIB/JDK dynamic proxy around the bean. Calling a method internally via `this.` does not go through the proxy, bypassing the TransactionInterceptor. Refactor by injecting self or moving to another bean.

spring-boot.questionText: Under 500 concurrent requests, HikariCP throws ConnectionTimeoutException. What is the architectural flaw?
options: RestTemplate cannot serialize JSON inside a transaction.
OrderRepository.save() closes the database connection prematurely.
Holding an open SQL connection while waiting for a slow external HTTP network call starves the database connection pool.
HikariCP does not support Spring Boot `@Transactional` annotations.
spring-boot.explanation: `@Transactional` acquires a JDBC Connection from the pool on method entry. Making external blocking HTTP network calls inside the transaction holds the connection open, exhausting pool capacity. Separate DB writes from external HTTP calls.

spring-boot.questionText: Iterating through 1,000 users triggers 1,001 separate SELECT queries to PostgreSQL. What is the optimal Spring Data JPA fix?
options: Change FetchType.LAZY to FetchType.EAGER on the `@OneToMany` mapping.
Use `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"orders_{0}"})` or a JOIN FETCH JPQL query to fetch users and orders in a single SQL query.
Replace PostgreSQL with a Redis key-value store.
Enable Hibernate 2nd-level cache without modifying queries.
spring-boot.explanation: Changing to EAGER still executes N+1 queries when using findAll(). `@EntityGraph` or `JOIN FETCH u.orders` instructs Hibernate to emit an SQL LEFT OUTER JOIN, retrieving all parents and children in a single round-trip.

spring-boot.questionText: If the requestMatchers order is reversed (`/api/**` before `/api/admin/**`), what security vulnerability occurs?
options: Any authenticated non-admin user can access `/api/admin/**` because the first matching rule (`/api/**`) evaluates and authorizes the request.
The SecurityFilterChain bean fails to instantiate at application startup.
Spring Security rejects all requests with HTTP 403 Forbidden automatically.
OAuth2 JWT validation is bypassed entirely.
spring-boot.explanation: Spring Security matches request rules in top-to-bottom first-match-wins order. Specific restricted paths (like `/api/admin/**`) must precede generic broad paths (like `/api/**`).

spring-boot.questionText: Why must legacy blocking I/O calls be wrapped with `subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())` in Spring WebFlux?
options: Running blocking operations on the Netty EventLoop thread blocks all other concurrent reactive requests on that CPU core.
Schedulers.boundedElastic() disables garbage collection during report generation.
Netty automatically scales event loop threads to 1,000 workers.
WebFlux controllers cannot return Mono without boundedElastic.
spring-boot.explanation: Netty event loops use a small fixed number of threads (equal to CPU cores). If a blocking call executes on an event loop thread, no other requests assigned to that event loop can be processed. Offload blocking work to Schedulers.boundedElastic().

spring-boot.questionText: After the 10-second open state expires, what determines whether the Circuit Breaker transitions to CLOSED or back to OPEN?
options: It remains in HALF-OPEN permanently until the microservice restarts.
It pings the database health endpoint via TCP.
It executes 5 trial probe requests; if the failure rate is below the threshold it transitions to CLOSED, otherwise it resets to OPEN.
It waits for a manual HTTP POST request from the admin operator.
spring-boot.explanation: In HALF-OPEN state, Resilience4j permits a configured trial number of probe calls (`permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState`). If their failure rate meets the threshold, it heals to CLOSED; if any fail above threshold, it reopens.

system-design.questionText: Why is Orchestrated Saga preferred over Choreographed Saga for complex distributed workflows with many microservice dependencies?
options: An Orchestrator provides a centralized state machine with clear compensation visibility, preventing cyclic event mesh deadlocks and event spaghetti.
Choreography is prohibited by ISO 20022 standards.
Orchestrator eliminates network communication between services.
Choreography consumes 100x more memory than orchestration.
system-design.explanation: In complex workflows, an orchestrator coordinates transactions centrally, tracks timeouts, and invokes compensating rollbacks predictably without tangled event dependencies. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: How does the Transactional Outbox pattern paired with Debezium CDC prevent data inconsistencies compared to dual writes?
options: The entity update and outbox record are committed atomically in the same local database transaction; Debezium streams WAL commits to Kafka with at-least-once guarantee.
It converts Kafka topics into relational database tables.
It eliminates the need for database transaction logs entirely.
It guarantees zero network latency across microservices.
system-design.explanation: Dual-writes fail if the DB commit succeeds but Kafka send fails. The Outbox pattern writes to the local DB table atomically, and Debezium tails the database WAL to publish events reliably. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: Under Raft consensus rules, why will a follower node refuse to vote for a candidate even if the candidate's term is higher?
system-design.codeSnippet:
// 5-Node Raft Cluster
// Node 1 initiates election with Term 4
options: If the candidate's log is less up-to-date (has lower last log term or shorter log length) than the follower's own log.
If the candidate's IP address is numerically higher than the follower.
If the follower has been online for more than 10 minutes.
If the candidate uses UDP packets instead of TCP.
system-design.explanation: The Raft Leader Completeness invariant requires that a follower grants a vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as the voter's own log (higher term, or same term with longer index). (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: How does the XFetch algorithm eliminate Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd) when a hot key expires under high concurrency?
system-design.codeSnippet:
// XFetch Algorithm:
// if ( -delta * beta * ln(random()) ) >= remaining_ttl -> trigger refresh
options: The probability of a background reader recalculating and updating the cache key increases asymptotically to 1.0 as TTL nears zero, refreshing the cache prior to actual expiry.
It drops all incoming traffic when the cache key reaches 0 TTL.
It locks all Redis shards to single-threaded sequential execution.
It forces the client browser to compute the database query.
system-design.explanation: XFetch probabilistically triggers early refresh based on computation cost (delta) and TTL. A single reader refreshes the cache ahead of expiration, preventing massive database thundering herds. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: Why is a Redis Lua script essential for distributed rate limiting across multiple app servers?
system-design.codeSnippet:
local key = KEYS[1]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local current = tonumber(redis.call('get', key) or '0')
if current + 1 > limit then return 0 else redis.call('incrby', key, 1) return 1 end
options: Redis executes Lua scripts atomically in its single-threaded event loop, preventing Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race conditions across concurrent servers.
Lua scripts execute inside the client's browser JavaScript engine.
Separate GET and SET commands are banned by HTTP/2.
Lua scripts store rate limit counters in CPU registers.
system-design.explanation: Separate GET and SET calls allow concurrent servers to interleave commands, exceeding rate limits. Lua scripts execute atomically in Redis without race conditions. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: Why do write-heavy distributed databases (Cassandra, RocksDB) utilize Log-Structured Merge-Trees instead of B-Trees?
system-design.codeSnippet: // LSM Pipeline: Append to WAL -> Insert into MemTable -> Flush to SSTables
options: LSM-Trees transform random disk writes into sequential append-only writes, maximizing disk throughput and minimizing disk write amplification.
B-Trees cannot store numeric floating point values.
LSM-Trees do not use persistent disk storage.
LSM-Trees perform random in-place updates directly on flash memory.
system-design.explanation: B-Trees perform random in-place disk page updates, causing heavy write amplification. LSM-Trees append sequentially to WAL and MemTable, periodically compacting immutable SSTables. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: How does the Kafka Transaction Coordinator prevent zombie producers from committing split-brain transactions after a network partition?
options: It increments the producer epoch for that transactional.id, causing brokers to reject any subsequent writes from the old producer instance with ProducerFencedException.
It blocks the old producer's IP address on the Linux kernel firewall.
It automatically deletes the target topic partition.
It forces all broker nodes to reboot.
system-design.explanation: When a new producer instance initializes with a transactional ID, the coordinator bumps the epoch. Any late writes from the old zombie instance are rejected with ProducerFencedException. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: What critical problem do Virtual Nodes solve in Consistent Hashing topologies?
system-design.codeSnippet:
// Hash Ring: 0 to 2^32 - 1
// Physical Nodes mapped to 150 Virtual Nodes each
options: They prevent hot-spot data skew by distributing token positions evenly across the hash ring, ensuring uniform load distribution when nodes join or leave.
They eliminate the need for hash functions.
They reduce network bandwidth to zero.
They convert distributed hash tables into single-node in-memory lists.
system-design.explanation: Without virtual nodes, a small cluster has uneven hash token distribution. Mapping each physical server to 100-200 virtual nodes creates a balanced, uniform distribution across the ring. (Bloom's Taxonomy Level 3: Application & Troubleshooting).

system-design.questionText: Why is the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC preferred over directly publishing to Kafka inside the service method?
options: PostgreSQL WAL logs run in memory and do not write to disk.
Debezium compresses JSON payloads using GZIP hardware acceleration.
Kafka cannot accept messages directly from Spring Boot REST controllers.
It eliminates dual-write partial failure anomalies by committing data and event atomically in a single local database transaction.
system-design.explanation: Dual writes to DB and Kafka cannot be coordinated atomically without 2PC. If the DB commits but Kafka publishing fails (or network drops), state is permanently inconsistent. The Outbox pattern makes DB the single atomic commit point; CDC guarantees at-least-once streaming to Kafka.

system-design.questionText: In an at-least-once message delivery pipeline, how does a unique database index on `message_id` guarantee exactly-once processing semantics?
options: Kafka brokers automatically delete duplicate messages before sending to consumers.
Duplicate deliveries encounter a unique constraint violation on the idempotency key, allowing the consumer to safely ignore duplicate execution.
The consumer thread is terminated and restarted with fresh offset.
PostgreSQL locks the entire database table during duplicate inserts.
system-design.explanation: At-least-once brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) can redeliver messages upon network timeouts or rebalances. Storing the idempotency key atomically with business updates guarantees idempotent execution and prevents duplicate charges/orders.

system-design.questionText: Why does the consumer group enter an infinite rebalance storm, halting message consumption?
options: Consumers cannot process messages concurrently on 12 partitions.
Kafka brokers run out of memory when max.poll.records is set to 500.
The consumer took longer than `max.poll.interval.ms` (45s > 30s) to call `poll()`, causing the coordinator to assume it died and trigger a rebalance.
ZooKeeper terminates consumer sessions after 10,000 messages.
system-design.explanation: If message batch processing exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms`, the Kafka coordinator considers the consumer dead, removes it from the group, and triggers a rebalance. Solution: decrease `max.poll.records` or increase `max.poll.interval.ms`.

system-design.questionText: How does the XFetch probabilistic early recomputation algorithm completely eliminate cache stampedes (thundering herds)?
options: It forces the database to write directly to CPU L2 cache.
It holds all HTTP requests in an OS semaphore queue until cache warms up.
It calculates a probabilistic early refresh before expiration: as TTL nears zero, the probability of a background refresh approaches 100%, without locking.
It stores 5 duplicate copies of the product in separate Redis cluster nodes.
system-design.explanation: XFetch probabilistically triggers a single early refresh as the TTL approaches expiration. This ensures the cache key is refreshed in the background before it expires, preventing thousands of simultaneous DB queries.

system-design.questionText: What is the root cause of this performance degradation in PostgreSQL and what is the fix?
options: PostgreSQL B-Tree indexes convert to Hash indexes after 100,000 updates.
PostgreSQL MVCC writes a new dead tuple version for every UPDATE; slow autovacuum tuning creates table and index bloat. Tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and fillfactor.
PostgreSQL buffer pool cache memory was cleared by the OS kernel.
The Linux OS ext4 file system ran out of directory inodes.
system-design.explanation: Postgres implements MVCC using append-only tuple versioning: an UPDATE inserts a new row and marks the old row dead. If Autovacuum is too slow, dead tuples accumulate, bloating heap pages and index B-trees. Solution: tune autovacuum vacuum thresholds and table fillfactor.
